personality_voice.book_baseline: McGonagall's personality in the books is built on a consistent and richly layered set of traits: strict authority delivered with dry wit, fierce loyalty to Gryffindor and to her students, a capacity for genuine warmth that she almost never lets show, emotional restraint that occasionally fractures under pressure, and an undercurrent of sardonic humor. She speaks in short, sharp, declarative sentences — commands, dismissals, sharp interrogatives — punctuated by rare bursts of warmth. Her voice is highly distinctive: she can praise Hermione with 'a rare smile,' mock Trelawney tartly ('That explains a great deal'), use biscuits as a disarming tactic with Harry, shed a tear while blowing her nose at the thought of Pettigrew, and shake with fury when Fudge brings a Dementor to Azkaban. She is simultaneously unbending and deeply feeling. Her inner life is rich: guilt over Snape ('This is all my fault'), admiration for Dumbledore mixed with the courage to challenge him, and a pride in her students that she carefully conceals but which leaks out at critical moments — openly backing Harry's Auror ambitions while Umbridge is in the room, sobbing at the Quidditch Cup win, crying when Hermione is Petrified. Her speech patterns are consistently brisk, with 'Quite,' 'Very well,' 'That is obvious,' and occasional devastating understatement ('Thirty-nine years this December'). The dry humor is a defining feature: she tells Harry she hopes he will 'try and win' after returning his Firebolt, she offers biscuits three times during the Umbridge confrontation, and she tells the class she has never had much patience with Divination before stopping herself mid-sentence. She also harbors a competitive streak around Quidditch that she cannot disguise — deliberately abstaining from homework assignments the week before a match.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve McGonagall's core personality with remarkable consistency across all eight entries. Her sharpness is intact in nearly every scene: she reprimands Wood and Harry briskly in PS, introduces herself as a cat with perfect timing, dispatches instructions in clipped sentences, and confronts Umbridge with full hauteur in GoF ('And what are you doing?'). Her wit survives — the 'I've always wanted to use that spell' moment in DH2 is book-authentic in spirit, and her dismissal of Snape in DH2 ('Our headmaster has done a bunk') has the dry deflation characteristic of the books. The Yule Ball scene in GoF, where she dances with Ron to teach him and delivers the 'lordly lion prepared to prance' speech while barely containing her own humor, is a strong film-original expansion that is tonally faithful to the character. Her emotional restraint cracking under pressure is preserved: she visibly shakes with rage at Fudge in GoF after the Dementor incident, she cries at the Quidditch Cup in PA (sobbing harder than Wood), and in HBP she offers a quiet, emotionally restrained scene to Harry at Dumbledore's office that preserves her warmth-through-formality register. The DH2 confrontation with Amycus Carrow — standing firm when spat on, using Imperio without flinching, calling Snape a coward — is fully faithful to the book characterisation.
personality_voice.difference: Two meaningful losses. First, several instances of McGonagall's sardonic inner commentary are compressed out in adaptation: the extended Umbridge confrontation in OotP (three biscuit offers, the 'there may be a new Minister for Magic' line, the 'I shall assist you to become an Auror if it is the last thing I do' speech) is reduced to a brief exchange. The full texture of her quiet subversion of Umbridge — telling Peeves the chandelier 'unscrews the other way,' feigning helplessness during the fireworks — is absent from the films. Second, her emotional complexity around Pettigrew ('I was often rather sharp with him. You can imagine how I — how I regret that now...') and the self-blame around Snape ('This is all my fault') are present in compressed form or slightly rebalanced, but not deeply explored. The guilty complexity of her Snape admission is present in HBP (she acts on the information that triggers the attack) but her verbal self-flagellation from the books is streamlined. These are minor losses from an otherwise very faithful characterisation.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core voice — clipped authority, dry wit, emotional restraint cracking at key moments, loyalty to students, sardonic relationship with sentimentality — is preserved in observable dialogue and behavior throughout all eight films. The losses are real but secondary: tonal layers that enrich the character without changing who she fundamentally is. A minor deduction is warranted for compression of the Umbridge confrontation, which removes her most extended solo showcase of wit, pride, and advocacy, and for the loss of the Pettigrew guilt passage. The score sits at the top of the 18–22 band.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: McGonagall in the books has a dense, multi-function narrative role. She is: the formal institutional authority figure who enforces rules while privately protecting students from worse; the competent adult presence whose trust Harry must sometimes circumvent; the head of Gryffindor who manages her house members' welfare; a key participant in school governance under both Dumbledore and Umbridge; a member of the Order of the Phoenix who acts independently (fetching the Weasley children after Arthur's attack, refusing the Dementor's admission to Hogwarts); a figure whose agency drives plot moments (confiscating the Firebolt, organizing the Time-Turner bureaucracy for Hermione, confronting Umbridge, securing the school during the Battle of Hogwarts). Crucially, she is also the character who calls Harry out of meals, assigns detentions with consequential stakes, runs Sorting, runs Quidditch team selection, conducts careers interviews, and manages OWL examination logistics. Her narrative agency in OotP is unusually prominent: the full Careers Interview scene is one of the most sustained examples of a supporting character actively advocating for Harry against institutional pressure, and the scene of her confronting Umbridge is itself a plot driver (it escalates the tension and defines the power dynamic). In DH, she takes over the school, organizes the defense, deploys students and staff, and issues the order to hold Hogwarts — she is the functional commander of the resistance.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: McGonagall's major structural functions are largely preserved in the films. She runs the Sorting ceremony in all years, she recruits Harry as Seeker, she disciplines for rule-breaking (the night-time detention in PS, the 50-point deduction), she confiscates the Firebolt in PA, she informs Harry about the Yule Ball in GoF, she confronts Umbridge in GoF over the ferret, and she commands the defense of Hogwarts in DH2 with the Piertotum Locomotor sequence and the direct confrontation with Snape. Her GoF role in the Barty Crouch Jr. reveal scene — standing guard, being dispatched to fetch Hagrid, maintaining order — is preserved. The DH2 battle sequence is particularly faithful: she organizes the evacuation, deploys Neville and Seamus, openly challenges Snape, sends the statues to defend the castle, and gives Harry the time he needs.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Several important agency moments are lost or reduced. (1) The full OotP Careers Interview confrontation — one of her most sustained acts of advocacy, standing up to Umbridge in Harry's defense while Harry is present, declaring she will make him an Auror 'if it is the last thing I do' — is entirely absent from the film. This removes a scene where McGonagall acts as Harry's champion against institutional oppression in a uniquely personal way. The film cuts from Umbridge's broader OotP arc to the battle, skipping this. (2) The Firebolt subplot in PA: McGonagall's role as the character who confiscates and tests the broom is present, but the extended negotiation (her repeatedly refusing to return it, Wood complaining to her, her responding 'As long as necessary, Wood') is compressed. The core beat survives. (3) In OotP, her role in alerting Dumbledore to Arthur's attack, coordinating with portraits, and organizing the Weasley children's transport is absent because the scene in Dumbledore's office is streamlined. (4) In GoF, her objection to Harry competing ('Put an end to it') and her active dissent from Snape's silence approach at the staff meeting is present and faithfully rendered in the film. The principal losses are concentrated in OotP, where her most sustained advocacy for Harry (the Careers Interview) is cut entirely.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The loss of the OotP Careers Interview is meaningful: it is the one scene in the entire series where McGonagall functions as Harry's active protector against institutional authority in a direct, verbally confrontational mode. Its removal does not transfer her function to another character — Harry simply lacks that advocate in the film — but it leaves a gap in her narrative agency. The DH2 sequences more than compensate in terms of command and action agency. The role is reduced but recognizable, landing at the top of the 14–17 band.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: McGonagall's motivations are remarkably clear in the books, though layered. She is motivated by institutional loyalty (to Hogwarts, to Dumbledore, to the proper order of education), by fierce protectiveness of her students, by a belief in rules as the scaffolding of a just society — but a belief she is willing to subvert when a higher moral principle demands it (protecting Harry from Umbridge, undermining Umbridge's authority by passively allowing Peeves to continue). She is also motivated by a personal code: she will not punish unjustly, she will not lie to her students if it can be avoided, and she carries guilt (Pettigrew, Snape) when she misjudges people. Her internal conflict is concentrated in OotP: she is visibly torn between following Ministry procedure and protecting Harry, between institutional loyalty and moral courage. The confrontation in which she tells Harry 'tread carefully around Dolores Umbridge' while privately doing everything she can to undermine Umbridge captures this conflict precisely. In DH, the conflict resolves: she commits fully to resistance, using Imperio on Amycus without apparent hesitation.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films capture McGonagall's primary motivations cleanly: institutional loyalty combined with protective care for students is visible throughout. Her GoF objection ('Potter is a boy, not a piece of meat') directly expresses her core motivation against those who would use Harry instrumentally. Her HBP scene at Dumbledore's office after his death ('You meant a great deal to him') suggests emotional investment beyond institutional role. Her OotP advice to Harry ('tread carefully') is present in the film. The motivation to protect Hogwarts and its students drives her DH2 behavior explicitly.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The films lose the internal conflict dimension significantly. The books present a McGonagall who is genuinely torn between procedure and protection, who feels guilt explicitly (the Pettigrew passage), who self-blames for Snape ('This is all my fault'), and who experiences the tension between institutional authority and moral courage as an active psychological struggle. In the films, she is resolute rather than conflicted. The GoF staff meeting, where she clashes with Snape's passive approach and openly advocates against using Harry as bait, is present, but the subtler, ongoing tension of OotP — where she tells Harry to comply with Umbridge while privately subverting her at every turn — is present in the broad strokes but not in the full texture. The guilt over Pettigrew and the self-blame over Snape are absent from the films. These are real motivational losses but they do not make her motivations incorrect or incoherent — they are simplified rather than changed.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The core motivations survive: protecting students, institutional loyalty with room for moral courage, personal integrity. The losses are in internal conflict texture — guilt, self-blame, the active psychological tension between procedure and protection. This places her in the 11–13 band: motivations simplified but fundamentally correct.

character_arc.book_baseline: McGonagall's arc across seven books is largely flat in the sense that her core values do not change — she is always principled, strict, loyal, and capable of moral courage. However, there is meaningful arc movement: in books 1–3 she is primarily the enforcer, the institutional voice. In books 4–5, she becomes increasingly an active opponent of institutional corruption (standing up to Fudge, protecting Harry from Umbridge). In books 6–7, she steps into a leadership vacuum and becomes the de facto commander of the resistance, culminating in her taking the headmistress's chair and organizing the Battle of Hogwarts. This is not a dramatic transformation of character but a progression from institutional authority figure to institutional rebel to resistance leader. The arc's resolution — her becoming headmistress while fighting Voldemort — is earned by everything that precedes it.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films largely preserve this progression. She begins as the enforcer in PS (transfiguring her desk, running Sorting, punishing rule-breaking), moves to active resistance against Umbridge in OotP (the Careers Interview aside, her defiance of the inspection, her subversion of Umbridge's authority), and culminates in DH2 as the commander of the Battle of Hogwarts. The DH2 sequence is the strongest sustained realization of her arc's endpoint: Piertotum Locomotor, the confrontation with Snape, the direction of battle strategy, the moment of openly calling Snape a coward. The HBP funeral scene — McGonagall lifting her wand in salute with the rest of the school — is a quiet and faithful beat of institutional grief.
character_arc.difference: The OotP segment of the arc is compressed: without the Careers Interview, one of the clearest demonstrations of her mid-arc transition from enforcer to advocate is missing. The arc's progression is still legible and present, but one of its most important steps is absent. This is a compression that affects the arc's completeness without fundamentally altering its direction or resolution.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is compressed but still faithful: the beginning, middle progression, and end are all present and recognizable. The missing OotP material removes one important step but does not invent a false arc or eliminate the arc's logic. This sits at 14: arc complete and faithful, with minor compression.

key_relationships.book_baseline: McGonagall's most important relationships are: (1) Dumbledore — a relationship of deep mutual respect, professional partnership, and occasional disagreement, where she is his most trusted lieutenant and feels his loss most acutely; (2) Harry — a relationship that evolves from strict assessor to protective advocate to, finally, something approaching maternal pride; (3) the institutional hierarchy — her relationship with Umbridge is one of barely contained contempt, with Fudge one of frustrated loyalty, with Snape one of professional cooperation that collapses into betrayal. The Dumbledore relationship is defined by scenes like the opening of PS (her deference to his wisdom, her challenge to his decisions), the GoF staff meeting (her active disagreement with Snape's approach while staying aligned with Dumbledore), the DH hospital wing (her devastated confession that she sent for Snape), and the DH2 office scene (quietly placing Harry's need above her own grief).
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Dumbledore relationship is preserved in its essential emotional beats: the PS opening scene (present and faithful), the GoF confrontation at the staff meeting (she opposes Snape's passive approach and sides with Dumbledore's caution), the HBP funeral (the wand salute), and the DH2 office scene ('You meant a great deal to him'). The Harry relationship is present across the films: the PS Seeker recruitment (warmth breaking through formality), the OotP advice scene, the DH2 'It's good to see you' exchange. The Umbridge antagonism is vivid in both GoF (the ferret confrontation) and the broader OotP dynamic.
key_relationships.difference: The OotP Careers Interview — the most intimate and sustained scene of McGonagall's relationship with Harry as his advocate — is absent, which removes the clearest expression of how far her protectiveness extends. The guilt-laden dimension of her relationship with Dumbledore, expressed in the books through her self-blame for summoning Snape and her devastated disbelief at Snape's treachery, is compressed but present. The relationship with Snape, defined by the books as professional cooperation built on Dumbledore's trust collapsing into betrayal and fury, is preserved in DH2 (the battle confrontation, calling him a coward). These relationships are mostly faithful with some compression.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Key relationships are mostly faithful in dynamic and tone, with the most significant loss being the extended Harry advocate dynamic of OotP and some of the guilt-texture of the Dumbledore relationship. The Umbridge, Snape, and Dumbledore relationships are all functionally preserved. Score in the 7–8 range: mostly faithful, with some compression.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: The books present a McGonagall of considerable complexity: she enforces rules she privately thinks are wrong; she can be simultaneously strict and compassionate within the same scene (Neville's grandmother scene in HBP — 'high time your grandmother learned to be proud of the grandson she's got' followed by practical schedule adjustments); she can giggle at a Christmas kiss from Hagrid and then correct herself; she can cry while blowing her nose briskly; she can feel genuine guilt and self-blame while maintaining composure. She has strong opinions that she restrains (Trelawney scenes — 'I shall not conceal from you that I have very little patience with it'), she has a competitive streak around Quidditch that borders on unseemly given her seniority, she is capable of using Imperio without hesitation when the stakes are high enough, and she carries a specific, named grief about Pettigrew and Snape that complicates her as a moral figure. Her humor is active and dry rather than incidental. The three biscuit offers during the Umbridge scene are emblematic: she is simultaneously playing a straight-faced institutional role and making a small act of defiance and comfort. This layering is what makes her more than simply 'the strict teacher.'
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve a meaningful amount of this complexity. The Yule Ball dance instruction scene is a strong example: she is formally instructing, internally amused at Ron's discomfort, committed to the ritual while recognizing its absurdity. The 'I've always wanted to use that spell' line in DH2 captures the dry humor and the woman underneath the institution. The PA Quidditch commentary interventions — her own hat falling off while she shakes her fist at Malfoy — preserve the competitive undercurrent. The HBP office scene with Harry after Dumbledore's death is emotionally complex: she doesn't know what to say, she falters, and she lands on 'You meant a great deal to him' — which is simultaneously impersonal and deeply personal. The DH2 use of Imperio on Amycus preserves her capacity for ruthless pragmatism.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The lost material is not trivial. The OotP Careers Interview removes the most extended exploration of her advocacy, humor, and capacity for open defiance. The Pettigrew guilt passage removes a moment of genuine moral complexity (regretting her sharpness toward someone she misjudged). The Snape self-blame removes her capacity for guilt and self-examination that complicates her authority-figure role. The full Umbridge inspection scene — where she turns her back and teaches over Umbridge's interruptions — is reduced. The specific texture of her relationship with Neville (the HBP schedule scene, 'high time your grandmother learned') is absent. The Three Broomsticks scene in PA, where she expresses admiration-tinged-with-regret about Pettigrew ('I was often rather sharp with him'), is absent. These are losses that simplify without flattening — she remains a complex figure, but with some of her most specifically textured moments removed.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The films deliver a recognizable and substantially complete McGonagall. The losses are real — the guilt and self-blame dimensions, the extended humor of the Umbridge confrontation, the Pettigrew nuance, the Neville relationship texture — but they do not reduce her to a single trait or a simplified function. She remains strict, dry, caring, loyal, and capable of moral courage in the films. This places her in the 11–13 band: minor loss of nuance, character remains substantially complete.

score_caps_applied: No caps applied. The total of 85 is within the appropriate range for a character whose core identity, voice, arc, and key relationships are substantially preserved, with meaningful but not fundamental losses concentrated in secondary texture and one significant scene (the OotP Careers Interview).
comparative.key_observations: McGonagall is one of the most faithfully adapted supporting characters in the Harry Potter film series. Her defining traits — clipped authority, dry wit, fierce loyalty, emotional restraint that fractures under pressure, and moral courage that ultimately overrides institutional compliance — are all consistently present across all eight films. The films are particularly strong in her DH2 material, where she serves as the resistance commander, and in her recurring use as a figure of dry institutional humor. The primary loss is the OotP Careers Interview scene, which is the most sustained and intimate showcase of her advocacy for Harry and her defiance of Umbridge. Secondary losses include the guilt-and-self-blame dimensions (Pettigrew, Snape), her Neville relationship texture, and some of the layered humor of the Umbridge confrontation. None of these losses change who she fundamentally is, but they do remove the most specifically complex material the books provide for her. The result is a portrayal that is recognizably faithful at high fidelity while lacking the full depth of her book incarnation.
